clue.text: Redhead's son went out, being very glum

indicators.note: out here means wrong or disordered, so the letters of the preceding words are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of these three words, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A red-haired woman is miserable now that her son has left home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'went out' reads as one phrase, but 'went' is part of the fodder and 'out' alone signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Being very glum is a state of dejection, which is exactly what the noun describes as low spirits.

clue.text: Party dress maiden and smug C-in-C re-designed for advisor

parts.note: a do is an informal word for a party
a mini is a short dress

indicators.note: redesigning something gives it a new form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: M is the cricket scoring abbreviation for a maiden over
taken as written
Commander-in-Chief, its letters taken without hyphens

explanation.surface: A fashion note: a party frock, a girl and a self-satisfied commander, all remade for a consultant.
explanation.walkthrough: Dominic Cummings was chief adviser to UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson, 2019-20.
explanation.definitionFit: He was a famous political adviser at Downing Street, so the word names him by his role.

clue.text: Protective finish for court and rebuilt lido

parts.note: to court someone is to woo them

indicators.note: rebuilding something puts its parts together anew, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A treatment for a sports court alongside a refurbished open-air pool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'court' looks like a noun (a tennis court) but works as the verb meaning to woo.
explanation.definitionFit: Wood oil is a coating rubbed into timber to protect and finish its surface.

clue.text: Face of awfully evil cheat

indicators.note: awfully suggests something badly done, so these letters are mangled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The countenance of a dreadfully wicked swindler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Face' looks like a human face, but in printing it means a typeface.
explanation.definitionFit: Helvetica is a widely used sans-serif typeface, and a typeface is called a face by printers.

clue.text: Lark averse to cold

parts.note: anti means opposed to

explanation.surface: A songbird that dislikes chilly weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lark' suggests the bird, but here it means a playful prank.
explanation.definitionFit: An antic is a piece of foolish or playful behaviour, which is what a lark means as a noun.

clue.text: Instructive sessions spilled out into tests

indicators.note: into means the jumbled letters go inside the other piece

parts.note: trials are tests

indicators.note: spilled suggests scattered contents, so the letters of the next word are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Classes where the results leak out into examinations.
explanation.definitionFit: Tutorials are teaching sessions with a tutor, so they are instructive meetings.

clue.text: Last to sing during calamitous lament

indicators.note: during means the letter sits inside the other word

parts.note: dire means disastrous or calamitous

indicators.note: Last to sing means the final letter of that word

parts.note: only its final letter is used, as Last to directs

explanation.surface: Singing last in a disastrous moment of mourning.
explanation.definitionFit: A dirge is a mournful song, a musical lament for the dead.

clue.text: Euphoria when family member runs away

indicators.note: runs away means the cricket abbreviation for runs is taken out of the word

parts.note: a relation is a relative

explanation.surface: Delight when a relative leaves home.
explanation.walkthrough: R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs.
explanation.definitionFit: Elation is great happiness and excitement, close to euphoria in meaning.

clue.text: Appeal by Wall's when cycling: 'O spend money! A tub!'

indicators.note: cycling sends things round and round, so these letters are turned over into a new order

parts.note: the letters of these words, punctuation ignored

explanation.surface: An ice-cream maker's slogan as a cyclist is urged to splash out on a tub.
explanation.walkthrough: Wall's is a British ice-cream brand whose vendors' tricycles carried the slogan 'Stop me and buy one'.
explanation.definitionFit: This was Wall's famous advertising slogan, an appeal to passers-by to purchase an ice cream.

clue.text: Doctor on-line with appeal bathed in glow

parts.note: MO is a Medical Officer
the first part of on-line, taken as written
it is slang for sex appeal

explanation.surface: An internet physician with charm, shining in the light.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on-line' looks like one word but splits into ON and L for line.
explanation.definitionFit: Moonlit describes something lit by the soft light of the moon.

clue.text: Rent trouble, quite a blow

parts.note: rent as past participle of rend means torn
ado is fuss or trouble

explanation.surface: Problems with paying the rent come as quite a setback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' suggests money paid to a landlord; here it means ripped.
explanation.definitionFit: A tornado is a violent windstorm, so it is quite a blow in the sense of wind.

clue.text: Not a soul at end of performance after midday

indicators.note: after puts the letter following the other piece

parts.note: noon is midday

indicators.note: at end of means take only the final letter of performance

parts.note: only its final letter is used, as at end of directs

explanation.surface: Nobody turned up when the show finished at lunchtime.
explanation.definitionFit: No one means nobody at all, which is what not a soul means idiomatically.

clue.text: Medicare provision originally organised — it's now or never

indicators.note: organised means set in a new order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: originally points to the first letter of provision

parts.note: only its opening letter is used, as originally directs

explanation.surface: Health-care provision must be sorted out urgently.
explanation.walkthrough: Medicare is the US government health-insurance scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: Carpe diem is Latin for 'seize the day', a motto urging action before the chance is lost.

clue.text: Cacti with eels swimming in waters off Southern Ireland

indicators.note: swimming suggests moving around freely, so these letters are shuffled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Desert plants and fish swimming together off the Irish coast.
explanation.definitionFit: The Celtic Sea is the part of the Atlantic lying south of Ireland.

clue.text: Parents' daily trip around lunch or so. Not usually!

indicators.note: around suggests turning the letters about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Taking the children to school happens around lunch, says the clue, then admits it does not.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not usually!' is the setter's aside: the school run is in the morning and afternoon, not at lunch.
explanation.definitionFit: The school run is the daily journey parents make taking children to and from school.

clue.text: Chinese bear on patrol?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the black-and-white bear of China
second meaning: a ... car, a British police patrol car

explanation.walkthrough: A panda car is British slang for a small police patrol car, once painted in blue and white panels.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the giant bear native to China and a police car on its rounds.

clue.text: Lots and lots of sheep and broken pieces of pottery

parts.note: pots means a large amount, as in pots of money
herds are large groups of animals

explanation.surface: Masses of sheep among smashed crockery.
explanation.definitionFit: Potsherds are fragments of broken earthenware, often found by archaeologists.

clue.text: Some soulful tragic radical

indicators.note: Some means only a part of the following words is taken

parts.note: the letters run across these two words

explanation.surface: A soul singer's sad extremist song.
explanation.definitionFit: An ultra is an extremist, someone holding radical views.

clue.text: Weeks at school in one or more stations

parts.note: a term is a period of weeks in the school year
taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: School weeks spent at one or more railway stations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one or more stations' reads as one phrase, but 'one' belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Termini is the plural of terminus, a railway station at the end of a line.

clue.text: He made assertion about independence held back

parts.note: taken as written from the start of the clue

indicators.note: about means the first word goes round the letter

parts.note: stated means declared or asserted

explanation.surface: A man declared something about independence but held back.
explanation.definitionFit: Hesitated means paused or was reluctant to act, so it means held back.

clue.text: Large quantity of gold in rear of coupe

parts.note: a tonne is a thousand kilograms
Au is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: A sports car loaded with gold in its back seat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link word here, not a containment signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A tonneau is the rear passenger section of an open car.

clue.text: The Merchant of Venice, maybe

definitions.meaning: surface: the Shakespeare play; setter: a trader from Venice
signals the cryptic reading: one such merchant

explanation.walkthrough: The capitals point to Shakespeare, but read literally the clue asks for a famous merchant from Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: Marco Polo was a thirteenth-century Venetian trader and traveller, a real merchant from that city.

clue.text: Bad feeling when leader's removed from platform

indicators.note: the leading letter is dropped from the start of the word

parts.note: a podium is a raised platform

explanation.surface: Resentment when the chief is ousted from the stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Odium is general hatred or disgust, a strong bad feeling.

clue.text: Hiding power of the ear and eye

indicators.note: Hiding means the ear word conceals the letter inside it

parts.note: otic is the adjective relating to the ear

explanation.surface: A hidden ability in both hearing and sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Optic is a humorous noun for the eye, the organ of sight.

clue.text: Believer in some faith in Dubai

indicators.note: some means only part of the following words is taken

parts.note: the letters run across these three words

explanation.surface: A follower of a religion living in the Gulf city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Believer in some faith' looks like the whole definition; 'Believer' alone defines and 'some' marks the hidden letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A Hindu is an adherent of Hinduism, a believer in that religion.

clue.text: I repeatedly snore — sadly making more din

indicators.note: something going sadly goes wrong, so the letters are put in a different order

parts.note: taken as written
repeatedly means the I is given again, so it appears twice
taken as written as fodder

explanation.surface: Someone confesses that their constant snoring unfortunately disturbs everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: Two Is (I 'repeatedly') join SNORE, and 'sadly' rearranges all seven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Noisier is the comparative of noisy, describing whatever creates a louder racket.

clue.text: Weapon from dump or depot

indicators.note: dump suggests tipping things out in a heap, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Munitions taken from an arms dump or store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dump' reads as a noun for a storage site, but signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A torpedo is a self-propelled underwater missile, a naval weapon.

clue.text: Attire for the Lido with roughly two GCSEs, minimum

indicators.note: roughly suggests an approximate shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Pool wear is available to anyone with at least a couple of school qualifications.
explanation.walkthrough: GCSEs are the exams English pupils sit at about sixteen; a lido is an open-air swimming pool.
explanation.definitionFit: A swimming costume is the garment worn for bathing at a pool.
